Visual Analysis: The image consists of two vertically stacked schematic diagrams used to illustrate fundamental principles of mechanics of materials, specifically regarding internal forces and stresses in a bar under axial load.

**Top Diagram:**
This diagram depicts a straight, prismatic bar (represented by a light-grey rectangle with a thick black outline) that has been theoretically cut into two segments along a vertical plane. Large red arrows labeled '$F$' point outward from the outer ends of both segments, indicating that the bar is subjected to an external tensile (pulling) force. At the interface where the cut was made, a series of smaller, parallel red arrows point outward from the right segment and inward toward the left segment. These smaller arrows represent the distributed 'surface forces' or stresses acting on the cross-sectional area. The Greek letter '$\\sigma$' (sigma) is placed centrally between the two segments, identifying these distributed forces as normal stress. The orientation of the arrows perpendicular to the cut surface signifies that these are normal stresses (Normalspannungen).

**Bottom Diagram:**
This diagram shows a similar configuration of a cut bar under the same external tensile forces '$F$'. However, instead of showing a distribution of many small arrows at the cut surface, it displays a single, larger red arrow on each side of the cut. These arrows are labeled '$N$' and represent the resultant internal normal force (Normalkraft). These internal forces act to maintain the equilibrium of each segment against the external force '$F$'.

**Visual Style and Relationships:**
The diagrams utilize a high-contrast color scheme with red for all force vectors and black/grey for the structural elements. The progression from the bottom diagram to the top diagram visually explains the relationship between the total internal normal force '$N$' and the intensity of that force per unit area, defined as the normal stress '$\\sigma$'. In the context of the provided text, this image specifically illustrates the determination of internal forces through a 'cut s-s' and the subsequent definition of technical stress according to Augustin Louis Cauchy, assuming a uniform distribution of stress across the constant cross-section.

chunk-61bee0456fb356f553c6809b0f9fb7ef.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\sigma = \frac {N}{A} = \frac {F}{A}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the fundamental definition of normal stress (Normalspannung) in a uniaxially loaded structural member, derived from Cauchy's stress principle. The equation establishes three equivalent expressions: σ = N/A = F/A, where σ denotes the normal stress acting perpendicular to the cross-sectional area, N represents the internal normal force resultant within the member obtained through the method of sections (Schnittverfahren), A is the constant cross-sectional area of the straight bar (Stab), and F is the external axial load whose line of action coincides with the bar axis (Stabachse). The equality N = F follows from equilibrium conditions applied to the free body diagram after making a cut s-s perpendicular to the bar axis. The equation embodies the assumption of uniform stress distribution across the cross-section, which is valid for bars with constant or weakly varying cross-sectional areas (schwach veränderliche Querschnittsfläche). This represents the elementary theory of tension/compression members, where positive values indicate tensile stress (Zugspannung) and negative values indicate compressive stress (Druckspannung). The relationship is foundational in strength of materials (Festigkeitslehre) and elasticity theory (Elastizitätsmodell), serving as the basis for more complex stress analyses. However, the context explicitly notes limitations: at bar ends, notches (Kerben), and geometric discontinuities, non-uniform stress distributions and stress concentrations (Spannungsspitzen) occur, requiring advanced methods beyond this elementary formula. The equation connects to kinematic relationships (Kinematische Beziehungen) through Hooke's Law and strain calculations, forming part of the broader framework of structural mechanics for analyzing load-bearing capacity and material behavior.

chunk-4e52c13f9f7327cff72c363dce5291e4.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\sigma (x) = \frac {N (x)}{A (x)}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation σ(x) = N(x)/A(x) represents the fundamental definition of the technical normal stress (Normalspannung) at a position x along an axially-loaded bar (Stab), rooted in Cauchy's stress theory. The numerator N(x) denotes the internal normal force (Normalkraft) at position x — that is, the resultant internal force acting perpendicular to the cross-section, obtained via the method of sections (Schnittverfahren) by passing a cutting plane s-s through the bar and enforcing equilibrium. The denominator A(x) is the cross-sectional area (Querschnittsfläche) at position x, which may vary along the bar's longitudinal axis. The quotient yields σ(x), the average normal stress distributed uniformly over the cross-section, expressed in units of N/mm² or MPa. By writing the equation as a function of the coordinate x, the formula generalizes the elementary theory of the prismatic tension/compression member to bars with weakly varying cross-section (schwach veränderliche Querschnittsfläche), where the assumption of uniform stress distribution remains a valid engineering approximation. Sign convention: for a tension member (Zugstab), N(x) > 0 produces positive tensile stress σ > 0; for a compression member (Druckstab), N(x) < 0 yields negative compressive stress σ < 0. The formula is central to cross-section dimensioning (Querschnittsbemessung): rearranging gives A_erf = |N|/σ_zul, providing the minimum required cross-sectional area so that the stress does not exceed an allowable value. Limitations noted in the surrounding text: the formula fails near bar ends, notches (Kerben), and geometric discontinuities where stress concentrations (Spannungsspitzen) produce non-uniform distributions that cannot be captured by elementary theory; slender compression members must also be checked for buckling (Knicken) failure, which may precede stress failure.

chunk-0fcadd4252fc137457a877dc2c0a4044.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\mid \sigma \mid \leq \sigma_{zul}\quad \text{zulässige Spannung}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation |σ| ≤ σ_{zul} represents the fundamental stress design criterion (Spannungsnachweis) in structural mechanics and strength of materials. Here, σ denotes the normal stress (Normalspannung) acting on a cross-section, computed as σ(x) = N(x)/A(x), where N(x) is the internal normal force and A(x) is the cross-sectional area. The absolute value |σ| ensures the condition applies to both tensile stress (positive, Zugspannung) and compressive stress (negative, Druckspannung), as seen in the conical bar example where N(x) = -F produces compression. The parameter σ_{zul} (zulässige Spannung) is the allowable stress—a material-specific limit defined by engineering codes that incorporates safety factors against yielding, fracture, or other failure modes. This inequality serves as the governing constraint for cross-section dimensioning (Querschnittsbemessung): the required cross-sectional area A_{erf} must be chosen such that the maximum stress magnitude anywhere in the component remains below σ_{zul}. In the context presented, this criterion is particularly important because non-uniform stress distributions due to geometric discontinuities (Kerben/notches, Stabenden/bar ends) create stress concentrations (Spannungsspitzen) that locally exceed predictions from elementary bar theory. The absolute value formulation is critical because failure criteria are typically based on stress magnitude rather than sign, though the context notes that slender compression members may fail by buckling (Knicken) before reaching σ_{zul}. This equation represents the simplest form of stress-based design verification, foundational to more complex failure theories (von Mises, Tresca, Mohr-Coulomb) used in machine design and structural engineering.

chunk-f2a6dab57c43d26f48e0a5a1f5535c85.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
A _ {e r f} = | N | / \sigma_ {z u l}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the fundamental dimensioning formula for required cross-sectional area in structural engineering design. The variable $A_{erf}$ denotes the 'erforderliche Querschnittsfläche' (required cross-sectional area), representing the minimum geometric area that ensures structural safety. $|N|$ represents the absolute value (magnitude) of the normal force (Normalkraft) acting along the longitudinal axis of the bar, whether tensile or compressive. The notation $\sigma_{zul}$ denotes the 'zulässige Spannung' (allowable/permissible stress), a material-specific limit value that accounts for safety factors against yielding, fracture, or other failure modes. The equation establishes an inverse proportionality: the required cross-sectional area increases linearly with the applied axial load and decreases inversely with the material's allowable stress capacity. The use of absolute value $|\cdot|$ ensures the formula is valid for both tensile and compressive loading scenarios, yielding a positive geometric area regardless of load direction. This represents a design constraint ensuring that the actual stress $\sigma = N/A$ does not exceed the permissible limit, i.e., $\sigma \leq \sigma_{zul}$. Within the surrounding context discussing stress concentrations at notches (Kerben) and bar ends (Stabenden), this equation applies to sections where Saint-Venant's principle holds—regions sufficiently distant from geometric discontinuities where stress distributions become approximately uniform. The context also references the conical bar example where $\sigma(x) = N(x)/A(x)$, establishing the relationship between this elementary theory and the dimensioning process. Notably, the text mentions that slender compression members may fail by buckling (Knicken) before reaching stress limits, indicating this equation applies primarily to compact cross-sections or tension members, with stability considerations addressed separately.

Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
r (x) = r _ {0} + r _ {0} \cdot \frac {x}{l} = r _ {0} \cdot \left(1 + \frac {x}{l}\right)
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation r(x) = r₀ + r₀ · (x/l) = r₀ · (1 + x/l) describes the linear variation of the radius along the longitudinal axis of a conical bar (truncated cone geometry). This is an affine-linear function defining the geometric profile of a pressure-loaded structural member.

**Mathematical Analysis:**
- r(x) is a continuous, monotonically increasing linear function of position x ∈ [0, l]
- Boundary conditions: r(0) = r₀ and r(l) = 2r₀, confirming the stated end radii
- The slope dr/dx = r₀/l is constant, characteristic of a cone with constant taper angle
- The dimensionless ratio x/l serves as a normalized coordinate parameter

**Variables in Context:**
- r(x): local radius of the circular cross-section at axial position x [m]
- r₀: initial (smaller) radius at x = 0 [m]
- l: total length of the conical bar [m]
- x: axial coordinate measured from the smaller-radius end [m]

**Physical & Theoretical Significance:**
This geometric function is foundational for computing the cross-sectional area A(x) = π·r(x)² and subsequently the normal stress distribution σ(x) = N(x)/A(x), where N(x) = -F (constant compressive internal force). Unlike a prismatic bar with uniform stress, the conical geometry produces a position-dependent stress field that is maximum where the cross-section is minimum (at x = 0). This exemplifies non-uniform stress distribution in variable-cross-section members.

**Application Domain:**
This equation belongs to Strength of Materials (Festigkeitslehre), specifically axial loading of bars with varying cross-sections. Such geometries appear in machine components (conical shafts), structural elements, and biomechanical models (e.g., bone geometry). The context notes that slender compression members may fail by buckling before reaching critical stress—a consideration for stability analysis.

chunk-cf7cfa532d0224ec6532c6354495df59.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\sigma (x) = - \frac {F}{\pi \cdot \left[ r _ {0} \cdot \left(1 + \frac {x}{l}\right) \right] ^ {2}}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the normal stress distribution σ(x) along the longitudinal axis of a conical compression rod (tapered bar) with circular cross-section. The rod has length l and end radii varying linearly from r₀ at one end to 2r₀ at the other end. The derivation follows from the fundamental definition of normal stress σ = N/A, where N is the internal normal force and A is the cross-sectional area. For this conical geometry, the radius varies linearly as r(x) = r₀·(1 + x/l), assuming x is measured from the smaller end. Substituting into A(x) = π·r(x)² and using the constant compressive internal force N(x) = -F (negative by sign convention for compression), we obtain σ(x) = -F/[π·r₀²·(1 + x/l)²]. The negative sign indicates compressive stress (Druckspannung). Key mathematical properties: the stress magnitude decreases quadratically with x, being maximum (most negative) at x = 0 with σ_max = -F/(π·r₀²) and minimum in magnitude at x = l with σ(l) = -F/(4π·r₀²) — a fourfold reduction. This non-uniform stress distribution, despite constant axial load, illustrates a critical concept in Festigkeitslehre (strength of materials): for non-prismatic members, stress concentration occurs at the minimum cross-section. This example directly relates to the chapter's discussion of Querschnittsbemessung (cross-section dimensioning) and Erforderliche Querschnittsfläche A_erf (required cross-sectional area). The equation is foundational for understanding the transition to subsequent topics on Dehnung (strain) and the relationship σ = E·ε (Hooke's Law), connecting stress analysis to elastic deformation behavior in slender structural members.

chunk-a453764f8253f8b0d724e7b0d2878c7c.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\sigma (x = 0) = 4 \cdot \sigma (x = l)
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation evaluates the normal stress function, $\sigma(x)$, at the two boundary points of an axially loaded conical bar, establishing a quantitative 4:1 ratio between them. In the context of solid mechanics, normal stress is defined as $\sigma(x) = N(x) / A(x)$. Because the bar is only subjected to a constant axial compressive force $F$, the internal normal force $N(x) = -F$ is uniform along the length $l$ of the bar. Therefore, the stress distribution is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area $A(x)$. Given the end radii are $r_0$ and $2r_0$, the circular cross-sectional area at the wider end is $\pi(2r_0)^2 = 4\pi r_0^2$, which is exactly four times the area at the narrower end ($\pi r_0^2$). By setting $\sigma(x=0) = 4 \cdot \sigma(x=l)$, the equation demonstrates that the normal stress at the narrower end of the bar ($x=0$) is four times greater in magnitude than the stress at the wider end ($x=l$). This illustrates a fundamental principle in structural design: stress concentrates in smaller cross-sections, which directly informs the required cross-sectional area ($A_{erf}$) needed to prevent material failure.

chunk-9650cbfdac35d71c763ff0baacdc1c9c.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\varepsilon = \frac {\Delta l}{l}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation $\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta l}{l}$ defines the technical (or engineering) normal strain, a fundamental kinematic quantity in continuum mechanics and strength of materials. 

- **Mathematical meaning and interpretation:** The equation represents a dimensionless ratio quantifying the average relative deformation of a one-dimensional body. It is a scalar value representing proportional change in length.
- **Variables and their definitions:** $\varepsilon$ is the technical strain (Dehnung), $\Delta l$ is the absolute change in length (Längenänderung, defined as final length minus initial length), and $l$ is the original undeformed length (Ausgangslänge) of the specimen or structural member.
- **Mathematical operations and functions used:** The equation utilizes a simple division (ratio) of the absolute deformation $\Delta l$ by the reference scalar $l$. 
- **Application domain and context:** This equation is situated within the domain of elastomechanics, specifically the kinematics of deformation. It directly follows the discussion of mechanical stress ($\sigma$) in a conical bar, bridging the gap between applied forces (kinetics) and the resulting geometric changes (kinematics).
- **Physical or theoretical significance:** Strain $\varepsilon$ indicates how much a material stretches (positive strain, $\Delta l > 0$) or compresses (negative strain, $\Delta l < 0$). Because it is dimensionless, it allows for the comparison of deformations across different scales and materials.
- **Relationship to other mathematical concepts mentioned in the context:** The surrounding text explicitly notes the restriction to small deformations ($|\varepsilon| \ll 1$), which is a necessary assumption for linearizing subsequent mechanical equations (such as Hooke's Law). Furthermore, this discrete, macroscopic formula is the conceptual precursor to the local, continuous formulation of strain given by the derivative of the displacement field, $\varepsilon(x) = \frac{du(x)}{dx}$, which is introduced immediately afterwards in the text for elements with variable cross-sections.
- **Practical applications or use cases:** Used extensively in structural engineering and material science to calculate length changes in columns, cables, and struts under load, and to determine material limits (e.g., yield strain).
- **How the equation relates to the broader discussion or framework:** This equation transitions the study from statics (internal normal force $N$ and stress $\sigma$) into the geometry of deformation (kinematics), laying the foundation for establishing constitutive laws (stress-strain relationships) that fully describe elastic body behavior.

Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\varepsilon (x) = \frac {d u}{d x} = \frac {\Delta l}{l}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the fundamental strain-displacement relationship in one-dimensional continuum mechanics, establishing the local strain field ε(x) as the spatial derivative of the displacement field u(x). The left equality ε(x) = du/dx defines strain in differential form, valid for position-dependent deformation where the displacement u(x) varies along the bar's longitudinal axis. The right equality du/dx = Δl/l connects this local definition to the engineering (technical) strain, which is the dimensionless ratio of total elongation Δl to original length l, applicable for homogeneous deformation. This equation is central to the kinematic description of deformation, operating under the small deformation hypothesis (|Δl| ≪ l or |ε| ≪ 1), which linearizes the strain measure. The equation is dimensionless and sign-definite: positive values indicate elongation (Δl > 0), negative values indicate compression (Δl < 0). Mathematically, it constitutes a first-order ordinary differential equation relating the displacement field to the strain field, enabling integration u(x) = ∫ε(x)dx to recover displacements from known strain distributions. Within the broader framework, this kinematic relationship provides the geometric foundation necessary for formulating constitutive laws (Stoffgesetze) that phenomenologically connect strains to stresses, ultimately enabling the analysis of elastic bodies under load through tensile/compressive testing and stress-strain diagrams.

chunk-89b8532cdf159a4bfe5be48dea8b78e2.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\rightarrow \sigma = F / A
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation $\sigma = F / A$ represents the fundamental definition of **mechanical normal stress** (Normalspannung) in continuum mechanics and strength of materials. Mathematically, it is a ratio of a scalar force quantity $F$ (the axial force, measured in Newtons [N]) to a scalar geometric quantity $A$ (the cross-sectional area, measured in mm² or m²). The result $\sigma$ has units of pressure, conventionally expressed in megapascals [MPa = N/mm²], as noted in the surrounding context regarding Young's modulus $E$.

**Variables and definitions in context:**
- $\sigma$ (sigma): mechanical stress — classified in the text as a *Kraftgröße* (force-related quantity), serving as a measure of material loading (*Beanspruchung des Materials*).
- $F$: axial force (Zug- oder Druckkraft), derived experimentally via tensile/compressive testing (*Zug- bzw. Druckversuch*).
- $A$: cross-sectional area (*Querschnittfläche*), which the surrounding text notes may be location-dependent (*ortsabhängig veränderliche Querschnittfläche*) when strain is not constant.

**Mathematical and physical significance:** This equation serves as the constitutive link between external loading and internal material response. It is the prerequisite for constructing the *Spannungs-Dehnungs-Diagramm* (stress-strain diagram) mentioned in the context. By normalizing force with respect to geometry, $\sigma$ becomes an intrinsic material measure independent of specimen dimensions, enabling comparison across different specimens.

**Relationship to broader framework:** The stress $\sigma$ is paired with strain $\varepsilon$ (defined kinematically via displacement $u(x)$), and together they form the two pillars of the constitutive model (*Stoffgesetz*). The surrounding lecture specifically targets the **linear-elastic regime** ($\sigma \leq \sigma_p$), where Hooke's Law applies: $\sigma = E \cdot \varepsilon$, with $E$ being the modulus of elasticity. The equation thus establishes the stress variable that, when related to strain, yields material parameters such as the elastic modulus and the yield stress $\sigma_F$ separating elastic from plastic behavior.

**Application domain:** Structural engineering, mechanical design, material characterization — used to determine whether a component's stress remains within admissible limits under load, and to classify material response as elastic ($|\sigma < \sigma_F|$) or plastic ($|\sigma > \sigma_F|$).

chunk-85da86ad0233986cf40614b65dc61ad2.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\rightarrow \varepsilon = \Delta l / l
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation $\varepsilon = \Delta l / l$ represents the fundamental definition of engineering strain (Technische Dehnung) in one-dimensional continuum mechanics. Here, $\varepsilon$ denotes the dimensionless strain quantity, $\Delta l$ represents the absolute change in length of the bar element (Stabelement), and $l$ denotes the original (undeformed) reference length. Mathematically, this is a normalized ratio that quantifies the relative elongation or contraction of a material body under mechanical loading. In the surrounding kinematic context, this global definition is extended to a local formulation where the displacement field $u(x)$ becomes position-dependent. The local strain is then derived as $\varepsilon(x) = du(x)/dx$, i.e., the first spatial derivative of the displacement function, and the displacement is recovered through integration: $u(x) = \int \varepsilon(x)\,dx$. This establishes strain as a kinematic quantity (kinematische Größe) describing the geometry of deformation, complementing stress (Spannung) as a force-related quantity (Kraftgröße). The strain definition serves as the kinematic foundation for constitutive models (Stoffgesetze), particularly Hooke's Law ($\sigma = E \cdot \varepsilon$), where the Proportionalitätsfaktor E (Elastizitätsmodul) linearly maps strain to stress within the linear-elastic regime ($\sigma \leq \sigma_p$). The equation is central to tension/compression testing (Zug- bzw. Druckversuch) and the construction of stress-strain diagrams (Spannungs-Dehnungs-Diagramm), distinguishing elastic recovery from permanent plastic strain ($\varepsilon_{pl}$) when the yield stress $\sigma_F$ is exceeded.

chunk-a093ad0a488172322e66eed43c540981.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\boldsymbol {\sigma} = \boldsymbol {E} \cdot \boldsymbol {\varepsilon}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the generalized Hooke's Law in tensorial notation, the foundational constitutive equation of linear elasticity theory. In the surrounding lecture context (German engineering mechanics / Festigkeitslehre, Section 10.3 'Stoffgesetz/-modell'), it describes the constitutive relationship between the second-rank Cauchy stress tensor σ and the second-rank linearized strain tensor ε, mediated by the fourth-rank elasticity tensor E (often denoted C_ijkl).

**Mathematical structure:**
- σ = (σ_ij) is the stress tensor, representing internal force intensities (units: MPa = N/mm²)
- ε = (ε_ij) is the infinitesimal strain tensor, the kinematic measure of deformation (dimensionless)
- E = (E_ijkl) is the fourth-order stiffness tensor satisfying minor symmetries (E_ijkl = E_jikl = E_ijlk) and major symmetry (E_ijkl = E_klij)

**Component form (Einstein summation convention):** σ_ij = E_ijkl · ε_kl

**Contextual interpretation:** The lecture distinguishes three behavioral regimes:
1. |σ| < σF → purely elastic (recoverable deformation)
2. |σ| > σF → elastoplastic (residual plastic strain ε_pl remains)
3. σ ≤ σp → linear-elastic (the focus of this course, governed by this equation)

The bold tensor notation indicates the equation's validity beyond the uniaxial rod case (Section 10.4 'Einzelstab'), encompassing biaxial and triaxial stress states. For the uniaxial bar element discussed subsequently, the equation reduces to σ = E·ε, where E is the scalar Young's modulus (Elastizitätsmodul), and the product EA constitutes the axial stiffness (Dehnsteifigkeit).

**Theoretical significance:** This linear mapping embodies the principle of material objectivity for small deformations and forms the constitutive kernel of the three-equation system for structural analysis: (1) equilibrium conditions, (2) kinematic relations, (3) material law. It is fundamental to displacement-based finite element formulations, where it defines the material stiffness matrix contribution to the global system K·u = F.

**For isotropic materials**, the fourth-order tensor E reduces to two independent Lamé parameters (λ, μ) or equivalently Young's modulus E and Poisson's ratio ν, expressed via the isotropic decomposition: σ_ij = 2με_ij + λε_kk δ_ij.

**Practical applications:** structural dimensioning, machine component design, civil engineering analysis, FEA simulations, and experimental characterization via tensile/compression tests (Zug-/Druckversuch) referenced in the lecture.

chunk-677c3b37a16b17c8907603bf39babaae.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\varepsilon = \sigma / _ {E}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation ε = σ/E represents the inverse formulation of Hooke's Law for uniaxial linear-elastic material behavior. Here, ε (Dehnung/strain) is the dimensionless kinematic quantity representing relative elongation, defined as the ratio of length change to original length. σ (Spannung/stress) represents the mechanical stress in [MPa = N/mm²], describing the internal force per unit area within the material. E denotes the Elastizitätsmodul (Young's modulus), a material-specific proportionality constant with units [MPa]. The equation establishes that strain is directly proportional to applied stress, with E serving as the inverse scaling factor. This relationship is valid only within the linear-elastic regime where σ ≤ σ_p (proportional limit stress), below the yield stress σ_F. Within the broader context of the Einzelstab (single rod) analysis framework described in section 10.4, this equation constitutes the third fundamental equation type—the elastizitätsmodell—complementing the Gleichgewichtsbedingung (equilibrium condition) and Kinematik (kinematics) equations. Together, these three equation systems enable determination of stresses and deformations in axially-loaded structural members. The term Dehnsteifigkeit (EA, axial stiffness) mentioned in the context represents the product of Young's modulus and cross-sectional area, directly derived from combining this constitutive law with equilibrium considerations. The equation forms the foundation for analyzing engineering structures under tension and compression loading.

chunk-6e2db8e0cc453f4ff50201dc37d1fa0c.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\begin{array}{c}\mid \leftarrow \mathrm{d} x \rightarrow \mid\\x \qquad x + \mathrm{d} x\end{array}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation depicts an infinitesimal rod element (differential element) of length dx along the longitudinal axis of a bar (Stab), with endpoints positioned at coordinates x and x + dx. This is a fundamental kinematic notation in continuum mechanics and structural analysis, used to isolate a differential segment of a one-dimensional load-bearing member for deriving governing differential equations. In the context of the surrounding lecture material on 'Einzelstab' (single rod analysis), this element serves as the basis for establishing the three foundational equation types: (1) the equilibrium condition (Gleichgewichtsbedingung) relating the internal normal force N(x) to distributed loads n(x), (2) the kinematic relationship (Kinematik) between displacement u(x) and strain ε(x) = du/dx, and (3) the constitutive law (Elastizitätsgesetz) based on Hooke's model with modulus of elasticity E. The notation |← dx →| visually emphasizes the infinitesimal length of the element, which is essential for formulating the differential equation dN/dx + n = 0 governing axial force distribution. This differential element approach enables the transition from discrete free-body diagrams to continuous field equations, ultimately yielding the rod's deformation behavior under various loading conditions including mechanical forces and thermal effects (ΔT).

chunk-f862d3f8b712d95184fc656859d1e6cd.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\rightarrow : N + d N + n \cdot d x - N = 0
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the infinitesimal equilibrium condition (Gleichgewichtsbedingung) for a one-dimensional bar element (Einzelstab) under axial loading. It is derived by analyzing a differential element of length dx extracted from the bar. The terms have the following meanings: N represents the internal normal force (Normalkraft) acting on the left face of the infinitesimal element at position x; (N + dN) represents the internal normal force on the right face at position (x + dx), where dN is the differential increment of axial force; n denotes the distributed line load (Linienkraft or Streckenlast) per unit length acting along the bar's longitudinal axis; and dx is the infinitesimal length of the element. The notation '→ :' indicates that equilibrium is being enforced in the axial (longitudinal) direction. Summing all forces in the bar's axial direction and setting them to zero for static equilibrium yields: N + dN + n·dx − N = 0. This equation is fundamental within the framework of the three equation types required to solve bar problems: (1) equilibrium conditions, (2) kinematic relations (describing strain-displacement), and (3) constitutive/elasticity laws (Hooke's model). Algebraic simplification gives dN + n·dx = 0, and dividing by dx yields the differential form dN/dx = −n. This result is central to deriving the governing differential equation for axial deformation of bars, particularly when combined with the kinematic relation ε = du/dx and Hooke's law σ = E·ε, ultimately leading to the bar's deformation equation involving the axial stiffness (Dehnsteifigkeit) EA. The equation applies to linear-elastic material behavior (σ ≤ σp) with focus on Young's modulus E measured in MPa. Physically, it expresses Newton's first law for a continuum element: the rate of change of internal axial force equals the negative of the applied distributed load, ensuring the bar element remains in mechanical equilibrium.

chunk-413d03b5c0b6ff01a4da279c609d09f9.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\frac {d N}{d x} + n = 0
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the differential equilibrium condition (Gleichgewichtsbedingung) for a one-dimensional bar element (Einzelstab) under axial loading in structural mechanics. The mathematical formulation states that the spatial derivative of the internal normal force N(x) along the bar's longitudinal axis x, plus the distributed line load n per unit length, must equal zero for static equilibrium. This is derived by analyzing an infinitesimal bar element: the difference between normal forces on opposing faces (dN) must balance the distributed load (n·dx) acting on that element. Variables: N(x) represents the internal axial normal force (Normalkraft) as a continuous function of position x along the bar; n represents the distributed line force (Linienlast/Streckenlast) with units of force per length [N/m]; x is the longitudinal coordinate. This equation constitutes the first of three fundamental equation types required to solve bar problems in the framework: (1) equilibrium condition, (2) kinematics relating strain to displacement, and (3) constitutive law (Hooke's model/Elastizitätsgesetz). In the special case mentioned where n = 0, the equation reduces to dN/dx = 0, yielding N = constant = F, meaning the normal force equals the applied end force throughout the bar. This equation is fundamental to the finite element formulation of bar elements and establishes the mathematical foundation for determining stress distributions σ = N/A and deformations in axially-loaded structural members.

chunk-faaf238bf3e3a6116edca46159e939df.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
F _ {1} = F _ {2} + n \cdot l
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation $F_1 = F_2 + n \cdot l$ represents the axial force equilibrium condition (Gleichgewichtsbedingung) for a single bar element (Einzelstab) subjected to both point forces and distributed line loads. Here, $F_1$ and $F_2$ denote the internal normal forces (Normalkräfte) at the two endpoints of a bar segment, $n$ represents the distributed line load (Linienkraft) measured in force per unit length [N/m], and $l$ is the length of the bar segment. The equation states that the normal force at one end equals the normal force at the other end plus the resultant of the distributed load integrated over the segment length. This is derived from static equilibrium ($\sum F_x = 0$) applied to a differential or finite bar element. In the broader context, this equation constitutes the first of three fundamental equation types needed to determine stresses and deformations in a bar: (1) equilibrium conditions, (2) kinematics relating displacement to strain, and (3) the constitutive law (Hooke's law). The term $n \cdot l$ is the integral of the distributed load $\int_0^l n(x)\,dx$ simplified for the case of uniform loading. This relationship is essential for constructing normal force diagrams (N-Verläufe) along the bar's longitudinal axis. The special case mentioned ($n = 0$, $\Delta T = \text{const.}$, $N = F$) reduces this to a constant normal force throughout the bar, simplifying subsequent stress ($\sigma = N/A$) and elongation ($\Delta l = Nl/EA$) calculations. This equation is foundational in structural mechanics for analyzing axially loaded members in trusses, columns, and other load-bearing components.

chunk-635877c2ca4bd8652a8de3e6ef23d5f9.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\varepsilon (x) = \frac {d u}{d x}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation is the fundamental kinematic relationship in one-dimensional continuum mechanics, defining the longitudinal strain field ε(x) as the first-order spatial derivative of the axial displacement field u(x) with respect to the longitudinal coordinate x. Mathematically, it represents the local gradient of the displacement function, capturing the rate of change of displacement per unit length along the rod's axis.

**Variables and Definitions:**
- ε(x): The longitudinal (normal) strain at position x, a dimensionless scalar field quantifying the local relative deformation (elongation or contraction per unit length). It is a kinematic quantity independent of material properties.
- u(x): The axial displacement field, measured in units of length [mm] or [m], describing the longitudinal displacement of the cross-section originally located at coordinate x.
- x: The Lagrangian (material) coordinate along the rod's longitudinal axis, measured in the undeformed reference configuration.

**Mathematical Operations:**
The equation employs the ordinary (total) derivative operator d/dx, which assumes a one-dimensional, uniaxial state of deformation. This derivative is well-defined provided u(x) is at least once differentiable (u ∈ C¹). For piecewise-defined displacement fields or at points of discontinuity (e.g., concentrated loads or material transitions), the derivative must be interpreted in a distributional or piecewise sense.

**Application Domain and Context:**
This equation appears within Section 10.4 'Einzelstab' (Single Bar), which establishes the three governing equation types required to determine stresses and deformations of a bar under axial loading:
1. **Gleichgewichtsbedingung** (Equilibrium condition): Relates internal normal force N to external loads
2. **Kinematik** (Kinematics): This equation ε(x) = du/dx, geometrically relating displacement to strain
3. **Elastizitätsmodell** (Elasticity model/Constitutive law): Hooke's law σ = E·ε, with the elastic modulus E and axial stiffness EA (Dehnsteifigkeit)

**Theoretical Significance:**
The equation embodies the **strain-displacement relation**, a cornerstone of geometric compatibility in solid mechanics. It is derived under the **small-strain assumption** (linearized kinematics), consistent with the linear-elastic regime (σ ≤ σ_p) emphasized in the surrounding material. Within this framework, the equation ensures geometric compatibility—the deformation field must be such that no gaps or overlaps develop in the continuum.

**Relationship to Broader Framework:**
Combining this kinematic relation with Hooke's constitutive law (σ = E·ε) yields σ(x) = E·du/dx, and further with the equilibrium equation (dN/dx + n = 0, where N = σ·A), produces the second-order governing differential equation for the displacement field: d/dx[EA·du/dx] + n = 0. For the special case of constant axial stiffness (EA = const.) and no distributed load (n = 0), this reduces to u''(x) = 0, giving the linear displacement distribution characteristic of a prismatic bar under end loads. Temperature effects (ΔT) introduce an additional thermal strain term ε_th = α·ΔT, modifying the constitutive relation to ε = σ/E + α·ΔT.

**Practical Applications:**
- Determination of stress distributions in axially loaded structural members
- Calculation of total elongation: ΔL = ∫₀ᴸ ε(x)dx = u(L) − u(0)
- Formulation of finite element stiffness matrices for truss and bar elements
- Analysis of statically indeterminate systems where displacement compatibility must be enforced
- Engineering design verification against proportional limits σ_p and yield stress σ_F to ensure elastic behavior.
chunk-635877c2ca4bd8652a8de3e6ef23d5f9.modal_entity_name: Kinematic Strain-Displacement Relation for Axial Deformation (equation)

chunk-3fb28b0e78717850205497e7c5e164dc.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\varepsilon = \frac {\sigma}{E} + \alpha_ {T} \Delta T
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the **generalized Hooke's law for thermoelasticity** in one-dimensional bar mechanics, decomposing total strain into mechanical and thermal components. The total longitudinal strain ε equals the sum of two independent contributions: (1) the elastic mechanical strain σ/E (classical Hooke's law), where σ is the normal stress and E is Young's modulus (Elastizitätsmodul), and (2) the thermal strain α_T·ΔT, where α_T is the coefficient of linear thermal expansion and ΔT is the temperature change relative to a reference state. This superposition principle holds under the assumption of linear-elastic, isotropic material behavior within the proportional limit (σ ≤ σ_p), consistent with the lecture's stated focus. In the surrounding context of 'Einzelstab' (single bar) analysis, this constitutive law (Stoffgesetz) serves as the third of three governing equation types—alongside the equilibrium condition (Gleichgewichtsbedingung) and kinematic relations (Kinematik)—required to solve for stresses and deformations in statically indeterminate systems. The thermal term becomes particularly critical in restrained structures, where thermal expansion is prevented, generating thermal stresses even under zero external load (a key phenomenon in engineering design). The equation simplifies to pure Hooke's law (ε = σ/E) when ΔT = 0, as noted in the context. This formulation is foundational for computing displacements of bar cross-sections and determining the deformation response under combined mechanical and thermal loading, with applications in structural engineering, mechanical design, and thermal stress analysis of constrained components.

chunk-794d30f8b956a266f2b6d66cc7f678de.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\frac {d u}{d x} = \frac {N}{E A} + \alpha_ {T} \Delta T
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the **differential constitutive relationship for a linear-elastic bar under combined mechanical and thermal loading** (thermoelastic bar equation). It expresses the axial strain ε as the first derivative of the displacement field u(x) with respect to position x.

**Mathematical interpretation:**
The left-hand side du/dx defines the axial strain ε(x) = u'(x), derived from kinematic considerations. The right-hand side represents the total strain as the **superposition of two independent strain contributions**.

**Variables in context:**
- u(x): axial displacement field of a bar cross-section [mm]
- x: longitudinal coordinate along the bar axis [mm]
- N: internal normal force (Normalkraft) [N], determined from equilibrium conditions
- E: Young's modulus / Elastizitätsmodul [MPa = N/mm²]
- A: cross-sectional area (Querschnittsfläche) [mm²]
- EA: tensile stiffness (Dehnsteifigkeit) [N], a compound material-geometric parameter
- α_T: coefficient of thermal expansion (Wärmeausdehnungskoeffizient) [1/K]
- ΔT: temperature change (Temperaturänderung) [K]

**Mathematical operations:**
The equation uses a first-order ordinary derivative (du/dx), rational expression (N/EA), and linear superposition. It constitutes a **first-order ODE** for the displacement field u(x), solvable by direct integration: u(x) = ∫(N/EA + α_T ΔT)dx + C.

**Physical significance:**
The first term N/EA represents the **mechanical strain** (mechanische Dehnung) due to axial loading. The second term α_T·ΔT represents **thermal strain** (thermische Dehnung) due to temperature change. This embodies the **superposition principle** for linear-elastic materials (Hooke's Law extended). The equation is valid within the proportional limit (σ ≤ σ_p) as stated in the context.

**Relationship to the framework:**
This is the third of three fundamental equation types for single-bar analysis (Einzelstab): (1) equilibrium conditions, (2) kinematics, and (3) the constitutive elasticity model. The context's special case mentions ΔT = 0, which reduces the equation to du/dx = N/EA. When additionally EA = const and N = F (constant), integration yields the classical elongation formula Δl = FL/(EA).

**Applications:**
- Computing bar deformations and displacements
- Thermal stress analysis in statically indeterminate systems
- Structural analysis of rods, columns, and truss members
- Mechanical engineering design under combined thermo-mechanical loading

chunk-2b12d2d988ba8fdb94bda0bb9243511d.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\sigma = \frac {N}{A}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation σ = N/A represents the fundamental definition of normal stress (Normalspannung) acting on a cross-section of a structural member, specifically a rod or bar (Stab) under axial loading. In this expression, σ denotes the normal stress with units [MPa = N/mm²], N is the internal axial force (Stabnormalkraft) determined from equilibrium conditions, and A is the cross-sectional area (Querschnittsfläche). This equation serves as the critical bridge between the first and third of the three fundamental equation types for analyzing a single bar: (1) the equilibrium condition (Gleichgewichtsbedingung) which yields the internal force N, (2) kinematics relating deformations, and (3) the elasticity model/law (Elastizitätsgesetz). Mathematically, it is a simple quotient expressing an intensive mechanical quantity (stress) as the ratio of an extensive force to a geometric area. Physically, it describes how the internal force distributes over the cross-section, assuming uniform distribution—a valid assumption for prismatic bars under centric axial loading. Within the broader context, this stress value is then compared against characteristic material limits discussed in section 10.3, such as the proportional limit σ_p (for linear-elastic behavior per Hooke's law), the yield stress σ_F (Fließgrenze separating elastic and plastic regimes), and is used in conjunction with Hooke's law σ = E·ε to determine strain and subsequently bar elongation via the axial stiffness (Dehnsteifigkeit EA). The equation is essential for engineering design, allowing verification that stresses remain within the linear-elastic range (σ ≤ σ_p), which is the stated focus of the lecture.

chunk-a7f547ed992922c6608475aa607ecc95.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\varepsilon = \frac {d u}{d x} \longrightarrow \Delta l = u (l) - u (0) = \int_ {0} ^ {l} \varepsilon \cdot d x \longrightarrow \Delta l = \int_ {0} ^ {l} \left(\frac {N}{E A} + \alpha_ {T} \Delta T\right) \cdot d x
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation chain represents the fundamental kinematic and constitutive relationships for axial deformation of a single rod (Einzelstab) in linear elastostatics. The derivation proceeds in three stages:

1. **Kinematic Relation** ($\varepsilon = \frac{du}{dx}$): Defines the longitudinal strain $\varepsilon$ as the spatial derivative of the displacement field $u(x)$ with respect to the axial coordinate $x$. This is a purely geometric relationship independent of material behavior.

2. **Integral Form of Elongation** ($\Delta l = u(l) - u(0) = \int_0^l \varepsilon \, dx$): Establishes that the total elongation $\Delta l$ equals the difference in displacements at the rod endpoints and equals the integral of strain over the rod length $l$. This connects pointwise deformation to global deformation.

3. **Constitutive Extension** ($\Delta l = \int_0^l \left(\frac{N}{EA} + \alpha_T \Delta T\right) dx$): Substitutes the generalized Hooke's Law including thermal effects. The total strain decomposes into:
   - **Mechanical strain**: $\frac{N}{EA} = \frac{\sigma}{E}$, where $N(x)$ is the internal normal force, $E$ is Young's modulus, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area. The product $EA$ is termed the axial stiffness (Dehnsteifigkeit).
   - **Thermal strain**: $\alpha_T \Delta T$, where $\alpha_T$ is the coefficient of thermal expansion and $\Delta T$ is the temperature change.

Within the surrounding context, this equation is central to solving statically determinate and indeterminate rod problems. The author emphasizes three equation types required: equilibrium conditions (Gleichgewichtsbedingung), kinematics, and the elasticity model. For statically determinate problems, $N(x)$ is found from equilibrium alone; for statically indeterminate problems, all three relationships must be solved simultaneously. The equation also illustrates that thermal expansion in unconstrained systems produces elongation without additional stress, while in constrained systems, thermal effects generate internal forces and stresses.

chunk-6fc1a89775e67ed1be0c24a11e1773f7.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\Delta l = \frac {F \cdot l}{E A} + \alpha_ {T} \cdot \Delta T \cdot l
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the total axial elongation (Δl) of a prismatic bar (Einzelstab) under combined mechanical and thermal loading. It is derived by integrating the strain-displacement relation ∫du = ∫ε dx along the bar's length under the special case conditions: constant tensile stiffness EA, no distributed axial load (n = 0), constant temperature change (ΔT = const.), and constant normal force N = F. The equation has two additive terms: (1) The mechanical component Fl/(EA), obtained via Hooke's Law where ε = σ/E and σ = N/A = F/A, integrated over length l; here EA denotes the Dehnsteifigkeit (axial/tensile stiffness). (2) The thermal component αT·ΔT·l, representing free thermal expansion (Wärmedehnung) due to a uniform temperature differential, with αT being the coefficient of thermal expansion. The equation embodies the three pillars mentioned in the surrounding context: equilibrium (Gleichgewichtsbedingung yielding N = F), kinematics (kinematic relation between displacement and strain), and the elastic/thermal constitutive model (Elastizitätsgesetz). In statically determinate systems, this thermal term produces only elongation without additional stresses, since the structure can freely deform. Conversely, in statically indeterminate systems, the same thermal expansion is constrained, inducing additional internal forces and stresses — a key conceptual distinction highlighted in the surrounding material. Variables: F = axial point load (Einzelkraft); l = bar length; E = Young's modulus (Elastizitätsmodul); A = cross-sectional area; αT = thermal expansion coefficient; ΔT = temperature change. This equation is fundamental in Festigkeitslehre (strength of materials) and Baustatik (structural analysis) for dimensioning load-bearing members, analyzing thermal prestressing, designing expansion joints in bridges and rails, and computing displacements in trusses and columns subject to environmental temperature variations.

Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
F = 0:
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation `F = 0:` represents a boundary condition or load case specification within the structural analysis of a single bar member (Einzelstab). In this context, it defines a specific scenario where the external axial force F acting on the bar equals zero at a particular location or cross-section. This is part of the three-equation framework for bar analysis: (1) equilibrium conditions (Gleichgewichtsbedingung), (2) kinematics, and (3) elasticity model (Elastizitätsgesetz). When F = 0, the normal force N(x) equals zero at that point, which directly affects the stress distribution σ = N/A = 0 and strain ε = σ/E = 0 at that cross-section. This boundary condition is particularly relevant for statically determinate problems where N(x) can be determined purely from equilibrium conditions. The condition may represent a free-end boundary, an unloaded section, or serve as a reference state for thermal loading analysis (Wärmedehnung). When combined with temperature changes ΔT, even with F = 0, thermal strains can develop: ε_thermal = α·ΔT. The colon notation indicates subsequent derivation of displacement equations u(x) under this constraint, integrating strain via ∫du = ∫εdx. This equation establishes the foundation for computing displacement fields and stress distributions in axially loaded structural members.

chunk-738c698a563cc3405e3c1de5794fa318.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\Delta l = \frac{\boldsymbol{F}\cdot\boldsymbol{l}}{EA}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the fundamental elongation formula for a prismatic bar (Einzelstab) under axial loading, derived from Hooke's Law. Mathematically, Δl denotes the change in length (elongation or contraction) of the structural member, F is the applied axial force (Einzelkraft), l is the original member length, E is Young's modulus (Elastizitätsmodul) characterizing material stiffness, and A is the cross-sectional area (Querschnittsfläche). The product EA is termed the tensile stiffness (Dehnsteifigkeit), a key parameter mentioned in the surrounding context. This equation emerges from integrating the three fundamental relationships discussed: (1) Equilibrium condition (Gleichgewichtsbedingung) yielding N=F for constant axial force; (2) Kinematics relating strain to displacement via ε=du/dx and Δl=∫εdx; and (3) The elasticity model (Elastizitätsgesetz) σ=N/A combined with ε=σ/E. Substituting these relationships produces ε=F/(EA), which integrated over length l gives Δl=Fl/(EA). The equation applies specifically to statically determinate problems with constant Dehnsteifigkeit and n=0, ΔT=0 (no thermal effects). For statically indeterminate systems or cases with thermal loading (ΔT≠0), additional compatibility equations and thermal strain terms must be incorporated. This formula is central to structural analysis (Baustatik), enabling engineers to predict deformations in columns, ties, struts, and truss members. It serves as the foundational relationship for understanding stiffness behavior in structural design and is the basis for more complex formulations involving variable cross-sections, distributed loads, or non-linear material behavior.

chunk-a371746d42ee15c97ccf2f983b9237ee.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\Delta l = \alpha_ {T} \cdot \Delta T \cdot l
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation $\Delta l = \alpha_T \cdot \Delta T \cdot l$ represents the **thermal expansion law** (Wärmeausdehnungsgesetz) for a prismatic bar, a fundamental constitutive relationship in structural mechanics. The variables are defined as follows: $\Delta l$ denotes the longitudinal change in length of the bar due to thermal effects; $\alpha_T$ is the coefficient of linear thermal expansion (Wärmeausdehnungskoeffizient), a material-specific scalar quantity with units [1/K]; $\Delta T$ represents the uniform temperature change applied to the bar [K]; and $l$ is the original length of the bar [m]. The equation describes a linear relationship between thermal strain $\varepsilon_T = \alpha_T \cdot \Delta T$ and the resulting elongation. Within the surrounding context of section 10.4 (Einzelstab), this equation forms part of the **kinematic relationship** connecting thermal effects to deformation. It is critical for distinguishing between statically determinate and statically indeterminate problems: for determinate systems, thermal expansion produces deformation $\Delta l$ without inducing additional normal forces or stresses ($N$, $\sigma$), as the structure can freely deform. For indeterminate systems, however, the constrained thermal expansion generates internal forces and additional stresses beyond the mechanical loading, requiring simultaneous consideration of equilibrium conditions (Gleichgewichtsbedingungen), kinematic compatibility (Kinematik), and the elastic constitutive law (Elasitzitätsgesetz with extensional stiffness $EA$). The equation establishes the thermal strain component that must be superimposed with mechanical strain $\varepsilon = \sigma/E = N/(EA)$ to obtain total deformation, typically integrated as $u = \int \varepsilon \, dx$ for variable cross-sections or loading conditions. This relationship is essential in civil and mechanical engineering for analyzing thermal stresses in constrained structures, bridge design, pipeline systems, and composite materials with differential thermal expansion.

chunk-c97b092fc202625d8ee8acd1894cf787.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
(E \cdot A \cdot u ^ {\prime}) ^ {\prime} = - n + (E \cdot A \cdot \alpha_ {T} \cdot \Delta T) ^ {\prime}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This is the governing second-order ordinary differential equation (ODE) for axial displacement of a single rod/bar (Einzelstab) under combined mechanical and thermal loading. It represents the synthesis of three fundamental principles of structural mechanics: equilibrium, kinematics, and the constitutive law (elasticity with thermal effects). The left-hand side $(E \cdot A \cdot u')'$ represents the spatial derivative of the axial stiffness times the mechanical strain, where $u' = \varepsilon$ is the derivative of displacement with respect to position $x$. The right-hand side contains the distributed line load $n = G/l$ (here representing self-weight as a constant Streckenlast) and the derivative of the thermal term $(E \cdot A \cdot \alpha_T \cdot \Delta T)'$. Variables: $E$ is Young's modulus (Elastizitätsmodul), $A$ is the cross-sectional area, $u(x)$ is the axial displacement field, $n$ is the distributed axial load per unit length, $\alpha_T$ is the coefficient of thermal expansion (Wärmeausdehnungskoeffizient), and $\Delta T$ is the temperature change. This equation is derived by substituting the constitutive relation $N = E \cdot A \cdot (u' - \alpha_T \cdot \Delta T)$ into the equilibrium condition $N' = -n$, yielding a unified formulation applicable to both statically determinate and statically indeterminate problems. The context specifically addresses a hanging bar under self-weight (Hängender Stab unter Eigengewicht), which is statically determinate, with boundary conditions $u(0) = 0$ (fixed support at top) and $u'(l) = 0$ (free, stress-free end at bottom). The equation is central to the finite element formulation for bar elements and demonstrates how thermal effects introduce additional stresses in statically indeterminate systems, whereas in statically determinate systems thermal expansion occurs without additional stresses.

chunk-0f197243eeecfe8da4e162edc85af353.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\frac {d u}{d x} = \frac {N}{E A} + \alpha_ {T} \Delta T
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the **kinematic constitutive relationship for axial deformation of a rod under combined mechanical and thermal loading**. It is a first-order ordinary differential equation relating the displacement field $u(x)$ to the internal normal force, material properties, and thermal effects.

**Mathematical Structure and Terms:**

- **Left-hand side $\frac{du}{dx}$**: The spatial derivative of the axial displacement function $u(x)$ with respect to the longitudinal coordinate $x$. This term equals the **total axial strain** $\varepsilon(x)$ of the rod.

- **Term $\frac{N}{EA}$**: The **mechanical strain** component, derived from Hooke's Law. Here, $N(x)$ is the internal normal force determined via equilibrium conditions, $E$ is Young's modulus (material stiffness), and $A$ is the cross-sectional area. The ratio $EA$ represents the **axial rigidity** of the cross-section.

- **Term $\alpha_T \Delta T$**: The **thermal strain** component, where $\alpha_T$ is the coefficient of linear thermal expansion and $\Delta T$ is the temperature change. This term captures free thermal expansion.

**Superposition Principle:**
The equation embodies the **superposition of strain components**: total strain equals mechanical strain plus thermal strain. This is valid under the assumption of small deformations and linear-elastic material behavior.

**Contextual Significance:**
Within the surrounding lecture material on 'Einzelstab' (single rod analysis), this equation serves as the **governing differential equation** for determining the displacement field. The lecture notes explicitly show the derivation chain: $\sigma = N/A \rightarrow \varepsilon = \sigma/E \rightarrow \int du = \int \varepsilon \, dx$. This equation combines these steps into a compact form.

**Statically Determinate vs. Indeterminate Systems:**
- For **statically determinate** systems: $N(x)$ is found from equilibrium alone, and thermal expansion causes displacement but **no additional stresses**.
- For **statically indeterminate** systems: The equation must be solved simultaneously with compatibility (kinematic) conditions and equilibrium equations. Thermal effects now **generate additional stresses** because the structure is constrained.

**Boundary Conditions and Integration:**
As shown in the example of the hanging bar under self-weight, this equation is integrated to obtain $u(x)$, with constants $C_1$ and $C_2$ determined from boundary conditions: $u(x=0) = 0$ (fixed support) and $u'(x=l) = 0$ (free end with zero strain).

**Assumptions:**
The context specifies constant values for $EA$ and $\Delta T$, which simplifies the equation to a form amenable to direct integration, yielding a polynomial or linear displacement profile depending on the distribution of $N(x)$.

chunk-b5cc011b4f71d9c304cbdecd2839b81e.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\frac {d N}{d x} + n = 0
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation $\frac{dN}{dx} + n = 0$ is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation representing the differential equilibrium condition for a one-dimensional structural element (rod or bar) subjected to a distributed axial load. Here, $N(x)$ denotes the internal normal force (Normalkraft) as a function of the longitudinal coordinate $x$, and $n$ represents a distributed line load (Streckenlast) per unit length. In the surrounding context, this distributed load arises from the self-weight of the hanging bar, where $n = G/l$ (weight per unit length, with $G$ being total weight and $l$ the bar length). Physically, this equation states that the spatial gradient of the normal force must exactly balance the applied distributed load for the infinitesimal element to be in mechanical equilibrium. Integrating yields $N(x) = -nx + C_1$, where the integration constant is determined by boundary conditions. This equation is the foundational equilibrium relation that, when combined with the kinematic relation $\varepsilon = du/dx$, the constitutive law (Hooke's law: $\sigma = E\varepsilon$), and the stress definition $\sigma = N/A$, produces the governing second-order differential equation for the displacement field $u(x)$ of the bar. It belongs to the classical framework of elastostatics and is particularly relevant for both statically determinate and indeterminate problems, as indicated in the lecture notes. The context specifies conditions $E \cdot A = \text{const.}$ and $\Delta T = \text{const.}$, making the equation directly integrable. For the hanging bar example, the boundary conditions $u(x=0) = 0$ (fixed support) and $u'(x=l) = 0$ (free end, zero strain) allow complete determination of the displacement, stress, and strain distributions. This equation is essential in structural mechanics, civil engineering, and mechanical engineering for analyzing axially loaded members such as columns, cables, bars, and rods under body forces or surface tractions.

chunk-f4f759f99f5a784630c625df026ca993.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
E \cdot A \cdot u ^ {\prime \prime} = - n
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation $E \cdot A \cdot u'' = -n$ represents the governing second-order ordinary differential equation (ODE) for the axial displacement field $u(x)$ of a one-dimensional structural member (rod/bar) under a distributed axial load. In this context: $E$ denotes Young's modulus (material stiffness), $A$ represents the cross-sectional area, $u'' = d^2u/dx^2$ is the second spatial derivative of displacement (related to strain gradient), and $n = G/l$ is the constant line load representing the bar's self-weight per unit length. The equation is derived by combining three fundamental principles of structural mechanics: (1) Equilibrium condition $N'(x) = -n(x)$, where $N(x)$ is the internal normal force; (2) Kinematic relation $\varepsilon = u'(x)$; and (3) Constitutive law (Hooke's law) $\sigma = E \cdot \varepsilon$, giving $N = E \cdot A \cdot u'$. Differentiating and substituting yields $E \cdot A \cdot u'' = -n$ when $E \cdot A = const$. The negative sign indicates that the distributed load acts opposite to the positive x-direction convention. This ODE is categorized as statically determinate in the surrounding context, meaning the internal forces can be determined from equilibrium alone. The boundary conditions provided ($u(0) = 0$ for fixed support and $u'(l) = 0$ for free end) complete the boundary value problem. Integration yields $u(x) = \frac{1}{EA}\left(-\frac{n}{2}x^2 + G \cdot x\right)$, from which elongation $\Delta l = u(l)$ and stress distribution $\sigma(x) = E \cdot u'(x) = \frac{G - n \cdot x}{A}$ can be computed. This equation is foundational in Festigkeitslehre (strength of materials) for analyzing axially loaded members and serves as the starting point for more complex statically indeterminate problems involving thermal effects and additional constraints.

Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
\Rightarrow E \cdot A \cdot u ^ {\prime \prime} = - n = - \frac {G}{l}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation is the governing ordinary differential equation (ODE) for the axial displacement field $u(x)$ of a single prismatic bar (Einzelstab) subjected to a constant distributed axial line load. The left-hand side, $E \cdot A \cdot u''$, represents the spatial derivative of the internal normal force $N(x) = EA \cdot u'(x)$, where $E$ is Young's modulus (Elastizitätsmodul), $A$ is the cross-sectional area, and $u'' = d^2u/dx^2$ is the second derivative of the axial displacement with respect to the longitudinal coordinate $x$. The right-hand side, $-n = -G/l$, encodes the constant distributed load (Streckenlast), where $G$ is the total weight force (Eigengewicht) and $l$ is the bar length. This ODE arises from combining the one-dimensional equilibrium condition $N'(x) + n(x) = 0$ with the linear-elastic constitutive law $N = EA \cdot \varepsilon = EA \cdot u'$. Under the stated assumptions $EA = \text{const.}$ and $\Delta T = \text{const.}$, the equation simplifies to a second-order linear ODE with constant coefficients. Integrating twice yields the general solution $u(x) = -\frac{G}{2EA \cdot l}x^2 + C_1 x + C_2$, where the integration constants are determined by the boundary conditions: $u(0)=0$ enforces zero displacement at the fixed (top) support giving $C_2=0$, and $u'(l)=0$ enforces zero strain (stress-free free end) at the bottom giving $C_1 = G$. The negative sign indicates the load direction relative to the chosen coordinate system (x measured downward from the fixed end). Physically, this describes a statically determinate hanging bar under self-weight, where the internal normal force varies linearly as $N(x) = G(1 - x/l)$, reaching maximum tension $G$ at the support and zero at the free end. This equation is foundational in Stabtragwerk analysis (structural bar analysis) and Festigkeitslehre (mechanics of materials), serving as the basis for computing stress distributions $\sigma(x)$ and elongation $\Delta l$ in axially loaded members, and it provides the mathematical framework that is later extended to statically indeterminate cases (e.g., beidseitig eingespannter Stab) where compatibility conditions supplement the equilibrium and constitutive equations.

chunk-17078647094adcc12a6785492579bc48.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
E \cdot A \cdot u ^ {\prime} = - \frac {G}{l} \cdot x + C _ {1}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the first-order ordinary differential equation (ODE) governing the displacement field of a hanging rod (Einzelstab) under self-weight in structural mechanics. Specifically, it is the integrated form of the bar's equilibrium differential equation. The left-hand side, $E \cdot A \cdot u^{\prime}$, represents the internal normal force $N(x)$ at position $x$, where $E$ is Young's modulus (Elastizitätsmodul), $A$ is the constant cross-sectional area, and $u^{\prime} = du/dx$ is the axial strain (Verzerrung). The right-hand side expresses the internal force as a function of position: the term $-\frac{G}{l} \cdot x$ represents the cumulative contribution of the constant line load $n = G/l$ (Streckenlast, weight per unit length), where $G$ is the total weight and $l$ is the rod length. The integration constant $C_1$ is determined by boundary conditions. From the context, the statically determinate hanging rod is fixed at $x=0$ (top) with $u(x=0) = 0$, and free at $x=l$ (bottom), where the strain vanishes: $u^{\prime}(x=l) = 0$. Applying this condition yields $C_1 = G$. Physically, at the fixed top end ($x=0$), the normal force equals the entire rod weight $G$ (maximum tension), while at the free bottom end ($x=l$), the normal force is zero. This equation derives from integrating the second-order equilibrium ODE $EA \cdot u^{\prime\prime} = -n = -G/l$ once. The assumption $E \cdot A = \text{konst.}$ and $\Delta T = \text{konst.}$ simplifies the governing equation to a linear form, neglecting thermal effects. This is part of the elastostatic analysis framework for axially loaded members (Stäbe), and serves as a foundation for solving statically indeterminate problems (e.g., beidseitig eingespannter Stab) discussed subsequently. The methodology connects to compatibility conditions ($\Delta l = \Delta l_1 + \Delta l_2 = 0$) and equilibrium conditions ($B - C = 0$) for more complex configurations. Applications include the design of cables, columns, hangers, and tensile structural elements where self-weight contributes significantly to stress distribution.

chunk-920d899bb09d20ddc75b79ec193db2e5.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
E \cdot A \cdot u = - \frac {G}{2 l} \cdot x ^ {2} + C _ {1} \cdot x + C _ {2}
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: The equation $E \cdot A \cdot u = - \frac{G}{2l} \cdot x^2 + C_1 \cdot x + C_2$ represents the general analytical solution (integral form) to the second-order linear ordinary differential equation governing the longitudinal displacement $u(x)$ of a one-dimensional structural member.

**Mathematical Meaning and Structure:**
The left-hand side isolates the product of axial rigidity ($EA$) and longitudinal displacement ($u$). The right-hand side is a second-degree polynomial resulting from the double integration of a constant axial load. The term $-\frac{G}{2l}x^2$ constitutes the particular integral accounting for the body force (self-weight). The terms $C_1x + C_2$ form the complementary (homogeneous) solution, representing rigid body translation and uniform strain modes. Structurally, isolating $EA$ on the left side is mathematically deliberate: taking the first derivative with respect to $x$ ('Ableitung nach $x$') directly yields the internal normal force equation $N(x) = EA \cdot u'(x) = -\frac{G}{l}x + C_1$.

**Variables and Contextual Definitions:**
- $E$: Young's Modulus (material stiffness).
- $A$: Cross-sectional area (assumed constant, $A(x) = konst.$).
- $u$: Longitudinal displacement at position $x$.
- $G$: Total weight of the rod (Gewichtskraft), not to be confused with the shear modulus. In this context, it defines a constant distributed line load $n = G/l$.
- $l$: Total length of the rod.
- $x$: Spatial coordinate along the longitudinal axis.
- $C_1, C_2$: Constants of integration determined by static boundary conditions.

**Physical and Theoretical Significance:**
In elastostatics, this equation mathematically predicts the deformation profile of a statically determinate ('statisch bestimmt') vertical member subjected to gravity. The parabolic nature of the $x^2$ term reflects the quadratic accumulation of displacement as the internal load integrates towards the fixed support.

**Relationship to Broader Framework:**
The surrounding text explicitly defines the boundary conditions for this 'Einzelstab' (single rod) example: $u(x=0) = 0$ (fixed top support, yielding $C_2 = 0$) and $u'(x=l) = 0$ (free bottom end, zero strain/stress, yielding $C_1 = G$). Substituting these constants provides the specific kinematic solution. This fundamentally contrasts with the subsequent 'statisch unbestimmt' (statically indeterminate) example, where solving for constants requires geometric compatibility equations (e.g., total elongation $\Delta l = 0$) in addition to equilibrium.

**Practical Applications:**
This formulation is foundational in structural engineering for computing axial deformations ($\Delta l$) and internal stress distributions ($\sigma = E \cdot u'$) in load-bearing components like suspension cables, vertical hangers, and columns, ensuring they satisfy strength and serviceability limit states.

chunk-460d07ec9180c3a338bcc5988e8e42a2.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
u (x) = \frac {1}{2} \frac {G l}{E A} \left(2 \frac {x}{l} - \frac {x ^ {2}}{l ^ {2}}\right);
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the axial displacement field u(x) for a statically determinate hanging bar (hängender Stab) subjected to its own self-weight (Eigengewicht). It is the solution to the second-order ordinary differential equation EA·u''(x) = -n, where n = G/l is the constant distributed axial load per unit length arising from the bar's self-weight.

Variables and definitions:
- u(x): Axial displacement at position x along the bar
- G: Total weight of the bar (self-weight), with distributed load n = G/l
- l: Total length of the bar
- E: Young's modulus (material stiffness)
- A: Cross-sectional area (constant along the bar)
- EA: Axial stiffness (assumed constant)
- x: Position coordinate (0 ≤ x ≤ l), measured from the fixed support

The dimensionless shape function (2x/l - x²/l²) captures the quadratic variation of displacement. The prefactor Gl/(2EA) represents the characteristic displacement scale.

Boundary conditions applied:
- u(x=0) = 0: Fixed support at the top (x=0), yielding integration constant C₂ = 0
- u'(x=l) = 0: Stress-free (free) end at x=l, yielding C₁ = G/EA

The maximum displacement occurs at the free end: u(l) = Gl/(2EA).

Differentiating gives the strain: ε(x) = (G/EA)(1 - x/l), and stress: σ(x) = (G/A)(1 - x/l). This shows maximum stress σ_max = G/A at the fixed support and zero stress at the free end, which is physically consistent with static equilibrium.

This solution belongs to the theory of elastostatics for one-dimensional structural members and is foundational for analyzing statically indeterminate systems, such as the thermally loaded, both-ends-fixed bar also discussed in the surrounding context.

chunk-a6e4242a538dfbd7e7ae0462ee78fbc7.content:
Mathematical Equation Analysis:
Equation: $$
N (x) = E A u ^ {\prime} (x) = G (1 - \frac {x}{l})
$$
Format: latex

Mathematical Analysis: This equation represents the axial force distribution (Normalkraftverlauf) N(x) in a vertically hanging rod under its own self-weight (Hängender Stab unter Eigengewicht). The equation combines the constitutive relation from linear elasticity (Hooke's law) with the equilibrium solution derived from the governing differential equation. Specifically: N(x) is the internal axial force at position x along the rod; E is Young's modulus (Elastizitätsmodul); A is the constant cross-sectional area (Querschnittsfläche); u'(x) = du/dx is the first derivative of the displacement function, representing the axial strain ε(x); G is the total weight of the rod (Gewicht); l is the total length; and x is measured from the fixed support at the top. The product EA·u'(x) represents the constitutive law where stress (σ = E·ε) multiplied by area gives internal force. The solution G(1 - x/l) shows a LINEAR distribution of axial force: at x = 0 (top support), N = G (maximum, carrying the entire rod weight); at x = l (free end), N = 0 (no load beyond the free end). This is consistent with the boundary conditions stated: u(0) = 0 (fixed support, zero displacement) yielding C₂ = 0, and u'(l) = 0 (stress-free free end, zero strain) yielding C₁ = G. The problem is classified as statically determinate (statisch bestimmt), meaning the support reactions can be determined from equilibrium alone. The constant line load n = G/l represents the weight per unit length. This equation is fundamental in structural mechanics for understanding stress distributions in axially loaded members and serves as the basis for calculating elongation Δl and stress σ in the rod.
